description: Systems engineer and master’s student from Türkiye. I work on radar and signal processing and used CW radar to detect human breathing behind walls and under debris for search and rescue. I am interested in SAR, Earth observation and disaster response. Skills: radar signal processing, MATLAB, Python, data analysis, machine learning. Solo team, but people interested in radar or remote sensing are welcome to message me!
summary: After a wildfire, hills turn green again within a few years, and optical satellites call the forest recovered. Most of that green is grass and shrubs. The Green Illusion uses NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar, which senses trunks and branches, to show how long a burned forest really needs. We combined MODIS burned-area maps (2001–2025), MODIS NDVI, NISAR GCOV images from summer 2026 and NASADEM elevation for about 4,670 km² of burned forest (21,754 squares of 500 m) from 27 fires in Antalya and Muğla (Türkiye), Evia (Greece) and the northern Sierra Nevada (California). In Mediterranean pine forests, optical data suggest 90% recovery after about 31 years; radar says about 67. In California, radar sees no steady return of trees, matching field reports of forest turning into shrubland. The web app lets anyone click any place on the map and get two dates for a fire today: when it will look green again, and when the trees will really be back. It also shows every past fire we studied, with an optical versus radar view. This matters for reforestation pledges, carbon accounting and recovery planning.
details:
What it does

The Green Illusion answers a simple question: if a forest burns, when does it really come back? It has two parts.

  • Try a place: click anywhere on the map and get two dates for a fire today. One is when the place will look green again from space (optical); the other is when the trees will really be back (NISAR radar). The estimate uses the elevation and slope direction of that point and the most similar forest type we studied.
  • Look back: 27 real fires since 2001 in Antalya and Muğla (Türkiye), Evia (Greece) and the northern Sierra Nevada (California), about 4,670 km² of burned forest, with how much has recovered by 2026 according to each sensor.

How it works

MODIS MCD64A1 gives each 500 m pixel its last fire date. For summer 2026 we took MODIS NDVI and NISAR L2 GCOV HV backscatter, which responds to wood rather than leaves. Each burned pixel is compared to unburned forest within 5 km. Fires of different ages measured on the same day form a recovery curve (space-for-time), fitted per forest type, with uncertainty from a bootstrap over whole fires. NASADEM elevation and aspect adjust the forecast for a chosen place.

Results

  • In Mediterranean pine forests (14 fires), optical data reach 90% recovery after ~31 years (29–36) and radar after ~67 years (49–109).
  • For the 2021 Manavgat fire, optical recovery is 32% and radar recovery is 13%. For the 2008 Serik–Taşağıl fire, 79% and 64%.
  • In California's Sierra Nevada, optical data say ~13 years, but radar shows no steady return of trees. This is consistent with documented conversion of forest to shrubland after severe fires.

Checked against field studies

Our satellite metric is not identical to field measurements, so we checked direction, not an exact match. In Spain, field plots 25 years after the 1994 fires found only 33 of 131 burned plots recovered to the level of unburned neighbors (Rodrigues et al. 2024). At 25 years our optical curve says 84% and our radar curve 58%, so the field result is much closer to radar. In Antalya, a field study of the same 2008 Serik–Taşağıl fire we analyse found no pine regeneration where young stands burned (Kavgacı et al. 2016). In California, field work documents forest turning into shrubland after severe fires (Richter et al. 2019), matching what NISAR shows.

Robustness check

Radar sees slopes differently depending on the viewing direction. For Antalya we also processed the NISAR pass from the opposite orbit direction on the same day (20 Aug 2026). The two views agree pixel by pixel (r = 0.85): Manavgat 2021 shows 13% vs 20% radar recovery, Serik 2008 shows 64% vs 67%, and time to 90% recovery is ~50 vs ~44 years. Both are far above the ~31 years from optical data.

Why it matters

Forest recovery is often judged by how green a burn scar looks. That can hide decades of missing trees, which affects reforestation reports, carbon credits and fire planning. NISAR covers almost all land every 12 days, through cloud and smoke, so this approach can scale worldwide.

Tools

Python (earthaccess, asf_search, h5py, pyhdf, numpy, scipy, pyproj, matplotlib), HTML/JavaScript with Leaflet, and GitHub Pages. No special hardware was used.

Limits

  • The long end of the curves is extrapolated; our oldest burns are about 25 years old.
  • Burn severity, soil and rainfall are not included yet.
  • Estimates far from the studied regions are rough, and the app tells the user. It also detects water and very high elevations.
